body: If confirmed, the move would be a vote of caution about AI customer finances from the company with the clearest view of chip demand. That would add weight to the circular financing debate that has hung over AI stocks this month. Custom chip designers and smaller AI players with stretched balance sheets would face tighter cash flow and could lose capacity to better-funded rivals. For TSMC, the policy would strengthen its pricing power and reduce its credit risk, a positive for the stock and for Taiwan’s tech-heavy market. Watch for any confirmation or denial from TSMC, which would set how seriously the report is taken. While Nvidia extends credit to the AI boom, TSMC is reportedly asking its customers to show the money first, and that difference says a lot about who carries the risk. TSMC has begun weighing customers’ finances before handing out chipmaking capacity, setting credit limits and asking some buyers to pay cash up front, Chinese technology outlet Kuai Keji reported, citing industry sources. TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet said it could not independently confirm it. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, is the world’s largest contract chipmaker. It does not design its own chips. Instead, it manufactures them for companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD and the growing number of firms building custom AI processors. Founded in Hsinchu in 1987, it produces the vast majority of the world’s most advanced chips. That gives it near-monopoly control of the capacity every AI company needs, and that leverage is what lets it set terms on who gets served first. According to the report, TSMC now sets a credit limit for each customer based on its balance sheet. The assessment reportedly covers any history of late or unpaid bills, the customer’s standing in the industry, its business outlook and the estimated loss if it defaulted. Orders above that limit must be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure their allocated capacity. The change is said to apply mainly to makers of custom AI chips, several of which are raising money through overseas convertible bonds, equity sales and syndicated bank loans. The report links the shift directly to concerns about circular financing in the AI industry, where companies invest in one another and then buy from each other. In effect, TSMC would be moving from allocating capacity on a first-come, first-served basis to asking customers to prove they can pay. That fits with comments from chief executive C.C. Wei, who has said on an earnings call that capacity planning takes into account cloud providers’ capital spending, their financial condition, and the availability of power and components. TSMC has also sent staff to the United States to check on data centre construction. The company already holds large customer prepayments, around NT$234 billion at the end of June, although Kuai Keji noted these are standard accounting prepayments rather than the new credit system. The contrast with Nvidia is striking. Nvidia is increasingly acting as a financier of the AI build-out, with commitments of about $518 billion and customer receivables of about $81 billion, according to its latest results and a Financial Times report. TSMC, sitting further up the supply chain with near-monopoly control of advanced chipmaking, appears to be heading the other way, shifting risk back onto its customers. If confirmed, the policy would tighten cash flow for chip designers that already tie up large sums in design and packaging costs, and it would favour well-funded customers over smaller players. body: Tokenized equities are still far too small to move BTC or ETH. The read-through is for listed crypto names tied to the sector, including Robinhood as an issuer and Coinbase as a venue for tokenized assets, and for the wider real-world asset story. If Nvidia’s post-earnings gains hold, most of the tokens minted near $156 will be in profit. That would help issuers argue that onchain demand rises with volatility instead of evaporating. The risk is redemptions into strength, which would shrink supply as quickly as it grew and weaken the case for tokenized stocks as a lasting home for retail risk appetite. While Wall Street sold Nvidia’s leadership crisis, onchain buyers minted more than a million new tokenized shares, and Kress’s first earnings beat gave them an early reason to feel good about it. Holders of tokenized Nvidia stock added to their positions as the chipmaker’s shares fell through the week of Jensen Huang’s resignation, with onchain supply rising 121% to about 2.3 million tokens, according to Token Terminal data shared by Token Relations. Over the same seven days, Nvidia’s share price dropped 13% to around $156. The timing also stands out. The data show supply starting to climb around November 9 and 10, after Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation on November 8 and before the November 12 announcement that Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive and director. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and Harvey C. Jones became the company’s first board chair. Most of the new supply came through bStocks’ NVDAb token, with xStocks’ NVDAx, Robinhood’s version and 15 smaller tokens making up the rest. Those buyers got an early test of their conviction overnight. As we reported, Kress’s first quarterly report since Huang’s departure topped forecasts by about $7 billion, and she pointed to a $2.5 trillion backlog while guiding for revenue growth of around 75% next year. Nvidia shares rose in after-hours trading. The episode offers a rare look at how onchain equity holders behave during a single-stock shock. The sums are small beside Nvidia’s market value of several trillion dollars, but the direction is clear: demand for tokenized exposure rose as the price fell. The next few sessions will show whether that was conviction or a short-term trade. If supply holds or keeps growing after the post-earnings bounce, issuers will have evidence that volatility brings in buyers. If holders redeem into strength, the surge will look more like a quick dip trade than a lasting shift. as a ps. if there is any demand for it I'll post up a separate explainer on all this. body: The Australian dollar barely moved, holding around 0.67, because traders treated the data as backward-looking and are focused on Thursday’s jobs report. Swaps still lean towards a peak in rates. A firm jobs number would challenge that, lifting front-end yields and supporting the currency, while a rise in unemployment would reinforce bets on easing by 2027. The contrast between strong wage growth and rising layoffs creates two-way risk for Australian bank stocks and rate-sensitive retailers, especially given the job cuts at David Jones and Bunnings. Watch the jobless rate on Thursday more closely than the headline jobs figure. --- Australia now has wages, interest rates and unemployment all rising together, which leaves the RBA choosing between the pay data and the layoff headlines. Australian wages grew at their fastest pace in nearly three years in the September quarter, giving the Reserve Bank of Australia more reason to keep policy tight even as cracks appear in the jobs market. The Australian Bureau of Statistics said its wage price index rose 1.1% in the quarter, the strongest result since late 2023. That broke a run of five quarters at around 0.8% and topped forecasts of between 0.9% and 1.0%. Annual growth picked up to 3.5% from 3.2%. Private sector pay rose 3.4% over the year and public sector pay 3.9%, Reuters reported. The ABS pointed to two drivers. The Fair Work Commission’s 4.75% increase in minimum and award wages from July lifted private sector pay, while raises for state government frontline workers pushed up public sector wages. Public sector pay has now outpaced the private sector for seven straight quarters. Real wages are still going backwards, down 0.4% over the year, the fourth consecutive quarter of decline. For the RBA, the harder question is what it may take to bring inflation down. If pay keeps rising at this rate, the bank may have to tolerate a jobless rate higher than it currently projects, possibly above the level it regards as consistent with steady inflation. The central bank has argued that the labour market is easing, yet pay growth shows little sign of cooling broadly. And unless productivity picks up, wage gains of this size sit uneasily with inflation returning to the 2% to 3% band. For households, at least, bigger pay rises offer some relief after a long squeeze. The bank lifted rates for a fifth time this year in November, to an 18-year high of 4.85%, partly because it judged the labour market to be a little tight. Three board members opposed the move, concerned the economy could be heading for a materially sharper downturn. One economist noted that Australia is in the unusual position of having unemployment, interest rates and wages all rising at once, and said wage growth and joblessness are likely to stay elevated through 2027. There are signs that the labour market is weakening. Unemployment hit a five-year high of 4.7% in September, and layoffs are spreading. Department store David Jones plans to cut 1,500 jobs by the end of the year, and hardware chain Bunnings said this week it would cut around 230 permanent roles. That puts Thursday’s employment report in focus. Forecasts point to a rise of 25,000 jobs in October and an unchanged unemployment rate of 4.7%. Markets largely looked through the wage figures, treating them as backward-looking. Swaps still imply about a 75% chance that the RBA has finished raising rates, with roughly 20 basis points of easing priced by the end of 2027. body: Record exports support the view that Japan’s economy can absorb a December rate hike despite the third-quarter contraction, which should keep upward pressure on short-end JGB yields. Chipmakers and chip equipment suppliers in Tokyo are the clearest beneficiaries, though the reliance on AI demand leaves them exposed to any pullback in global tech spending. Oil is the swing factor for the trade balance: crude prices tied to the Iran war set the size of Japan’s import bill, and a renewed spike would quickly widen the deficit. The yen is likely to take its direction from US-Japan rate gaps rather than the trade figures. --- Japan is selling more than ever to an AI-hungry world, but record oil-driven import costs mean households are not sharing in the boom. Japan’s exports rose for a 14th straight month in October and hit a record value, as global investment in artificial intelligence kept demand for chip-related shipments strong, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday. Exports climbed 20.5% from a year earlier to about ¥11.8 trillion, roughly $74 billion and the highest for any single month on record, Reuters reported. That beat the 20% median forecast and picked up from September’s 16.5% gain. Shipments to the United States rose about 24%, while exports to China increased about 13%. Analysts cited by Reuters said AI-related demand continued to support exports of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment, helping offset sluggish Chinese demand. Economists also noted that companies passing on higher costs had lifted the nominal value of shipments, so part of the gain reflects prices rather than volumes. Imports also set a monthly record at about ¥12.2 trillion, up 21.6% from a year earlier, although that was below the 25.8% forecast. Elevated crude prices and higher transport costs pushed up the value of energy imports amid instability in the Middle East, even as import volumes slipped 0.2%. Oil remains Japan’s main exposure to the Iran war, since the country imports close to 90% of its energy. The softer than expected import bill left a trade deficit of around ¥477 billion, about half the shortfall economists had forecast. The data shows external demand is still supporting an economy that contracted unexpectedly in the third quarter, as higher living costs forced households to cut spending. Rising import costs are likely to keep squeezing household purchasing power and corporate margins, which means the export boom is not translating into broad domestic strength. For the Bank of Japan, the figures add to the case for raising rates in December. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the bank will keep raising its policy rate in line with economic, price and financial developments, and that financial conditions remain accommodative. The policy rate is 1.25%. Resilient exports help offset the weak GDP reading, while import-driven inflation keeps pressure on the bank to act. The yen has drawn little support so far. USD/JPY remains near 160, where Tokyo has warned about intervention, as the rate gap with a Federal Reserve on a hiking path dominates. The risks to the export run are a slowdown in AI investment and further escalation in the Middle East, which would lift the oil import bill again. Your market education doesn't end here. body: The narrower deficit is mildly supportive for the yen because it reduces the yen sold to pay for imports. Rate differentials still dominate, though, and USD/JPY remains pinned near 160 while the Fed is on a hiking path. Oil is the key swing factor: Japan’s import bill is highly sensitive to crude prices during the Iran war, so any renewed rise in oil would quickly reverse today’s improvement. For the BOJ, the data adds to evidence that the economy can absorb a December hike, which could nudge short-end JGB yields higher. Exporters with heavy chip exposure should find support in Tokyo trade. Chips lifted Japan’s exports and a lighter import bill halved the expected trade gap, but the yen is still taking its cue from Washington, not Tokyo. Japan’s exports rose 20.5% in October from a year earlier, slightly ahead of expectations and a clear pick-up from September’s revised 16.5%, Ministry of Finance data showed on Wednesday. Chip shipments led the gain, ending a two-month slowdown in export growth. Imports rose 21.6%, well short of forecasts of about 26%, after an 18.5% rise in September. As a result, the trade deficit came in at around ¥477 billion. That was roughly half the ¥1 trillion or so analysts had expected and narrower than September’s revised ¥557 billion. On a seasonally adjusted basis, the deficit was around ¥767 billion, smaller than forecast but wider than the previous month. The import figure is the surprise. The government had said crude procurement would recover in October to around year-earlier levels as tankers routed through the Suez Canal arrived, so a bigger jump in the import bill was widely expected. Energy is Japan’s main vulnerability in the Iran war. The country imports close to 90% of its energy, and high oil prices have kept its import bill elevated. The data adds a modest tailwind to the Bank of Japan’s case for raising rates in December. The central bank held its policy rate at 1.25% in October, but Governor Kazuo Ueda signalled strong prospects for a hike at the next meeting after declaring that underlying inflation had reached the 2% target. Board member Hajime Takata said this week that rates should rise nimbly. Solid exports help offset a slight contraction in third-quarter GDP, and a narrower trade deficit means fewer yen are being sold to pay for imports. That may not be enough to lift the yen on its own. USD/JPY is trading around 159.5, just below the 160 level where Tokyo has stepped up warnings about intervention. With the Federal Reserve on a hiking path and US 10-year yields above 5%, the rate gap still works against the yen even if the Bank of Japan hikes. The 10-year JGB yield is near 2.9%, close to its highest since late October. The next test is Friday’s national inflation data. A firm reading alongside today’s trade figures would strengthen expectations for a December move. A rise in oil prices, on the other hand, would quickly push the import bill and the deficit back up. body: U.K. inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October, its highest level in a year, as fuel costs continued to rise. The reading was in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and marked an increase from September's print of 3.5%. Britain's Office for National Statistics said the largest contributor to the rising inflation rate was motor fuel costs, which rose 33.2% year-on-year. It was the largest one-year rise in motor fuel prices since July 2022, when energy costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The U.K. is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks such as the one sparked by the disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices have retreated from their wartime highs of well above $100 a barrel, but remain elevated. The ONS said Wednesday that the average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence (7 cents) per liter between September and October this year, compared with a 0.7 pence per liter rise in the same period a year earlier. The average petrol price stood at 174.7 pence per liter in October, the highest it's been since Aug. 2022. Diesel prices rose by 7 pence per liter in October, with the average price reaching 199.5 pence per liter — the highest since ONS records began in 1996. The Iran war has seen energy costs surge in various major economies. U.S. diesel prices hit $6 per gallon for the first time ever in September. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, inflation has risen sharply after a brief dip thanks to an energy price cap that was revised upward in July. Earlier this month, the Bank of England hiked interest rates for the first time in three years, warning that inflation could hit 5% by mid-2027. Governor Andrew Bailey said in the bank's November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside." Markets are currently pricing in around an 80% chance of a rate hike at the Bank of England's final meeting of the year. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JPMorgan Personal Investing, said in a note following the release that a recent climb down in oil prices following the U.S. midterm elections could offer some relief in future inflation readings. But he added: "While this may be a short-term reprieve for motorists, the broader outlook for UK inflation remains challenging as we approach 2027. After hiking interest rates at the start of the month, the Bank will be wary of a sustained uptick in inflation that could be here to stay."

Although October's inflation reading could be higher, softer fuel prices could help bring inflation down in November and December, before it continues to moderate through 2027. title: Fed officials set to raise rates again in December, but the future still looks murky
summary: continued inflation above the Fed's 2% target might push officials into a more aggressive stance.
body: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation , saying the central bank needs to "shock people" as prices continue to rise more than he expected. In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half percentage point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee. He said the central bank needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more. "I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a " Squawk Box " interview. "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions." Futures prices are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the FOMC's December meeting. They also are anticipating another move in January, followed by at least one additional increase before the end of 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Waller said the Fed wouldn't necessarily have to approve a half-point hike in December if it raised rates by a quarter point and signaled another move coming in January. However, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on grounds that it ties policymakers' hands. "If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets, you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 [basis points] in December to put it in place and get it done," he said. Recent statements from other central bankers indicate a range of opinions , though most agree that more policy tightening is needed to bring down inflation. In a speech Tuesday, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027. Some Fed officials, including regional Presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Lorie Logan of Dallas, have endorsed more gradual tightening. However, continued inflation above the Fed's 2% target might push officials into a more aggressive stance. The FOMC approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years in September, and then held rates steady at its October meeting. While inflation has continued to run hot since then, other Fed officials seem less eager to drop the policy hammer as heavily as Waller. "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday in a conversation with Axios. "I think what we've been doing over the last past few months is ... working well. We're collecting the data, analyzing it, having the debate and making a decision." The Fed in 2025 approved three rate cuts amid worries over the labor market and the belief that inflation would continue to moderate toward the central bank's 2% goal. However, inflation reignited earlier this year after the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran in late February. Energy prices spiked while tariff impacts lingered, keeping most inflation readings above 3% . "First of all, you've got to take back the three insurance cuts we put in last year," Waller said. "If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn't bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn't going to bring it down. So we may have to go above ... three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down." The FOMC later Wednesday will release minutes from the October meeting.

title: Mortgage demand turns lower, as interest rates shoot back up to the highest level in three weeks.
summary: Mortgage rates moved sharply higher last week, causing demand for both mortgage refinances and home purchase loans to drop. Rates hit the highest in 3 weeks.
body: Mortgage demand had been improving, as interest rates fell for about a month, but that came to an abrupt end last week. Mortgage rates moved sharply higher, causing total mortgage application volume to drop 2.3% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased last week to 7.35% from 7.21%, with points rising to 0.79 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. That was its highest rate in three weeks. "Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA. Applications to refinance a home loan fell 2% for the week and were 54% lower than the same week one year ago. The report comes as Nvidia has been rocked by the resignation of its CEO, Jensen Huang , after reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who worked for Singapore-based Megaspeed , which is being eyed by U.S. investigators for potential diversion of Nvidia's chips to China. "China is seeking to evade U.S. export controls to gain the most advanced semiconductors that underpin its intelligentization drive," the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said in its 2026 annual report to Congress. China is making that move as it faces a quality gap between chips produced by Chinese companies, including Huawei and Cambricon , and the more advanced ones produced by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, such as Advanced Micro Devices , the report noted. The report's findings could fuel concerns about advanced Nvidia chips having found their way to Chinese users amid escalating investigations from Congress and state and federal regulators. "Although China has made some progress in achieving its goals, it has not yet closed the hardest chokepoints — including the most advanced capabilities in logic fabrication, memory, and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, as well as the Nvidia Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) software moat — and likely will not for some time," the report said. "The resulting gap in compute is substantial, largely due to U.S. export controls on advanced chips," the report said. The report highlighted the fact that in the meantime, Chinese companies have obtained remote access to Nvidia chips through data centers in third countries, including Malaysia. On Tuesday, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued a rule intended to cut off that workaround. The move came in response to criticism from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Congress members that the Commerce Department had not done enough to prevent Nvidia's most advanced chips from being diverted to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission was created by Congress in 2000 with a mandate to monitor and report to Congress the national security implications of the trade and economic relationship between the U.S. and China.

The index is benchmarked so that 100 equals the average level of contract activity in 2001, a year NAR considers a normal, balanced market. Economists use the index to gauge where existing home sales are headed. The relationship isn’t perfect. Some contracts fall through because of financing problems, failed inspections or appraisal gaps, and cancellation rates can rise when mortgage rates jump or buyers get cold feet. Contract signings are highly sensitive to mortgage rates, so the index often responds quickly to moves in Treasury yields. A drop in rates can show up in pending sales within weeks, well before it appears in closings or prices. The report rarely moves broader markets, but it’s watched closely by homebuilder and mortgage-related stocks and as an early read on housing demand. In recent years, the index has hovered near historically low levels as high mortgage rates, stretched affordability and the lock-in effect, where homeowners are reluctant to give up low-rate mortgages, have kept buyers and sellers on the sidelines. He said the U.S. operation that removed Maduro in January lasted 48 minutes. Under an agreement reached in August , North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) holds 100-year concessions over 17 Venezuelan oilfields with an estimated 65 billion barrels of reserves. Washington receives a 35% equity stake in the company and the right to buy 20% of its oil output at cost. NABEP produces about 200,000 bpd and plans to reach 500 ,000 bpd by the end of 2028. body: Rystad Energy is an independent energy consulting services and business intelligence provider offering global databases, strategic advisory and research products for energy companies and suppliers,… The Democratic Party’s sweep of the US midterm elections is unlikely to derail Venezuela’s near-term oil recovery, but greater congressional scrutiny could slow the next wave of investment. Growth from existing fields should continue to support production of around 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) by 2028, up from 1.2 million bpd today. The risk, however, lies in greenfield developments, where Rystad Energy scenarios show delays to selected projects could leave output around 17% below the upside case by 2040. Democrats secured control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate in the 3 November midterm elections, and winners will take office on 3 January 2027. The incoming Congress is likely to increase scrutiny of Trump administration agreements with Caracas, particularly their transparency, legal foundations and long-term implications. Sanctions implementation and licensing by the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) remain largely under the president’s direction. The more immediate consequence for upstream investment is therefore likely to be additional review and potentially slower approval of newer agreements rather than a reversal of the reopening. Most near-term growth continues to come from existing fields, where operators can reactivate wells, carry out workovers, add infill drilling, and make targeted infrastructure investments. These projects generally require shorter lead times and are less dependent on large new approvals or long-dated investment decisions. Rystad Energy’s current commercial outlook sees production moving towards 2 million bpd in the early 2030s, but sustaining growth beyond this level increasingly depends on a new cycle of greenfield investment. Rystad Energy assessed three scenarios to quantify the drivers of Venezuela’s production outlook. The first reflects the current commercial outlook. The second combines a stronger price environment with continued policy support, under which Venezuela could approach 3 million bpd by 2040. The third retains those economic assumptions but applies greater scrutiny to selected longer-cycle developments, reducing the country’s production to around 2.5 million bpd by 2040. Greater scrutiny does not change Venezuela’s underlying resource potential, but it could change when some of those barrels reach the market. Some new oil developments require prices of around $80-100 per barrel under current fiscal terms. Proposed fiscal changes, combined with efficiencies in capital and operational expenditures, could bring some of these developments back into the investable range. Exposure to greater scrutiny will also vary significantly among operators. Proposed Venezuelan elections in 2027 add another layer of uncertainty, as a future elected government could revisit contracts or fiscal reforms introduced under the interim administration. Beyond 2035, Venezuela’s path towards 3 million bpd rests increasingly on long-cycle greenfield investment and on both the US and Venezuelan policy frameworks remaining sufficiently stable to support those commitments. title: Central banks rethink gold as global risks mount
summary: A new OMFIF report examines shifting reserve strategies, digital gold technology and retail investors' influence on prices.
body: Central banks are increasingly weighing geopolitical uncertainty alongside traditional financial risks when managing gold reserves, while new technology and retail investors reshape how the precious metal is held and traded, according to a new report by the Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum (OMFIF). The report , Holding power: How reserves, technology and investors are reshaping the gold market , draws on four confidential working group meetings held throughout 2026. It examines the competing priorities influencing reserve management amid a more fragmented and volatile global economy. The findings suggest gold’s role is becoming more complex as central banks balance diversification objectives against emerging geopolitical vulnerabilities, while technological advances create new opportunities to use existing holdings. However, the report cautions that innovations such as tokenization cannot automatically replicate the characteristics that make physical gold attractive to central banks, particularly as investor behaviour adds another layer of uncertainty to the market. Diversification remains the primary reason central banks hold gold, with most institutions citing portfolio rebalancing or the need to maintain target allocations. Although central banks generally rejected geopolitical risk as the main driver of their purchases, they acknowledged that the distinction between conventional financial threats and geopolitical vulnerabilities is becoming increasingly blurred. The findings build on OMFIF’s 2024 report, Gold and the new world disorder , which explored changes in central bank gold policies and the motivations behind official purchases. The latest research broadens that analysis to examine the operational, technological and environmental dimensions of gold ownership, alongside the implications of geopolitical developments. Tokenization could make gold easier to transfer, pledge as collateral and deploy across financial markets, potentially improving the efficiency of existing reserves without requiring central banks to change their strategic allocations. Faster settlement and automated collateral processes could also make gold more accessible for financial transactions. Yet the benefits of digital infrastructure come with limitations. Greater technological convenience does not necessarily preserve the security, control and other qualities that central banks associate with physical ownership. While most individual investors buy gold to preserve wealth over the long term, the report identifies a smaller segment of active traders whose transactions can amplify price movements and contribute to volatility. That distinction complicates the assumption that retail demand consistently provides stability to the gold market. Taken together, the findings point to a market in which gold’s traditional role as a reserve asset is increasingly intersecting with financial innovation and changing investment behaviour. The report suggests that central banks and market participants will need to assess not only why they hold gold, but also how evolving financial systems could affect its use, liquidity and strategic value. title: Critical mineral shortages threaten AI’s next growth wave: report

body: Artificial intelligence’s rapid expansion could run into a critical mineral supply crunch as demand for copper, lithium and rare earths outpaces mining production, threatening the infrastructure needed to support the technology, according to new research from Global X. The investment manager’s Charting Disruption 2027 report forecasts that mined demand could exceed supply by 17% to 22% across the three mineral categories by 2035. A single one-gigawatt AI data centre could require nearly 180,000 tonnes of critical materials, including about 27,200 tonnes of copper. The findings point to a widening gap between the speed of technological development and the mining industry’s ability to deliver raw materials. New mines take an average of 10 to 18 years to develop, leaving producers struggling to respond to demand from data centres, power grids, electric vehicles and advanced manufacturing. Global X research analyst Madeline Ruid said access to essential resources is becoming increasingly difficult as technological adoption accelerates. Concentrated mineral supply chains, lengthy project development timelines and water constraints could raise costs, delay construction and expose infrastructure projects to geopolitical disruptions. The challenge could shift investor attention beyond semiconductor manufacturers and technology companies towards miners, mineral processors and energy infrastructure developers. Securing reliable supplies of industrial metals is becoming increasingly important to the next phase of AI investment. Copper stands out as a key material because of its widespread use in electrical wiring, transformers, transmission networks and cooling equipment. Expanding AI computing capacity requires more than constructing data centres; it also depends on upgrading the electrical systems that supply them. Global X estimates that the copper, lithium and rare earths industries could require nearly $550 billion in investment through 2040 to meet growing demand and address supply chain vulnerabilities. The broader requirement for critical minerals and water infrastructure could exceed $2 trillion over the same period. Supply risks extend beyond the availability of mineral deposits. Production and processing are concentrated in relatively few countries, exposing manufacturers to trade restrictions, geopolitical tensions and disruptions that can affect access to refined materials. Rare earths are particularly important for permanent magnets used in industrial equipment, electric motors and other advanced technologies. Lithium remains central to battery storage systems that can help balance electricity supply as grids accommodate additional demand. Higher projected consumption does not guarantee shortages or sustained price increases, the report warns. New discoveries, recycling, substitution and improvements in processing efficiency could ease pressure on some commodities. Mining companies also face permitting delays, financing constraints and construction costs that can undermine project economics. body: California-based Earth AI has uncovered a copper-gold and platinum-group metals system stretching more than 3 km at its Fontenoy project in New South Wales, Australia, reviving a discovery that earlier explorers dismissed as small and discontinuous more than half a century ago. The company has completed 35 diamond drill holes totalling 20,919 metres, according to results released by project partner Legacy Minerals (ASX: LGM). Earth AI is moving to secure an 80% stake in Fontenoy and is funding additional drilling to support the project’s first mineral resource estimate under Australia’s JORC reporting standards. “Everyone asks AI exploration companies to show them a real deposit,” Earth AI founder and CEO Roman Teslyuk said. “Fontenoy is ours. The critical minerals shortage is mostly a search problem. The easy deposits were found a century ago by people who could see them.” The discovery comes as the US seeks alternative sources of critical minerals amid growing demand from data centres, electricity grids and defence industries. Global exploration spending runs at about $14 billion annually, according to Earth AI, even as the number of significant discoveries has fallen by roughly 70% over the past decade. The copper-gold zone, known as Meridian, was first drilled in 1969 and revisited in 1997. Both campaigns concentrated on shallow targets and interpreted the mineralization as scattered, relatively small occurrences. Earth AI’s geologists and artificial intelligence models instead identified the potential for a larger, continuous mineralized system. Its Alpheus model flagged Meridian in January and the company began drilling five weeks later. The company has since drilled 13,621.6 metres at Meridian, tracing copper-gold mineralization from near surface to depths exceeding 478 metres along approximately 3 km of strike. Historic drilling suggests the system could extend as far as 8 km, although that potential remains unconfirmed. Legacy previously described its 2024 discovery there as the first greenfield palladium discovery made using AI. Despite the expanded mineralized footprint, Fontenoy does not yet have a reported mineral resource. Further drilling and geological modelling will be needed to establish tonnage, grade continuity and the deposit’s potential economic viability. body: New U.S. export rules could slow Southeast Asia's data center boom by tightening access to advanced AI chips and targeting the region's role in providing computing power to Chinese companies. According to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department, data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips, including those from Nvidia. Facilities already serving large Chinese customers will have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions, the rule said. The region has seen a surge in data center construction to house the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models. U.S. restrictions on China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips have pushed Chinese technology firms, including Alibaba Group and ByteDance, to rent computing capacity in overseas data centers. About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026, according to October estimates by the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based think tank. The buildout has come under greater scrutiny as Washington presses ahead with the investigation into Nvidia 's former CEO Jensen Huang . Huang left the company that he co-founded in 1993 after reports of several alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy who is believed to facilitate billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips into China. The new restrictions will likely make building and operating these data centers "slower and costlier," said Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. The rules could undercut the business model of neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing — in the region, she said. Operators are likely to face more rigorous regulatory and national security requirements, said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. Greater scrutiny over investment into these projects could also weigh on Asian economies that have benefited heavily from the region's data center build-out. Malaysia stands to lose the most from the new restrictions, analysts say, given the scale of capacity being built in Johor and the sector's reliance on Chinese customers. More than half of Malaysia's data center capacity is in colocation facilities with Chinese firms accounting for "a sizeable share of these workloads," said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics. Commodity prices have also fallen recently, worsening Brazil’s terms of trade with the rest of the world,” she said. “All of this plays a role, but it pales in comparison with the shift in risk premiums on Brazilian assets since the election.” Damico added that criticism from within the ruling Workers’ Party (PT) of the “Moretti plan”—already deemed insufficient by financial markets—has heightened investor concerns, putting additional pressure on the real. body: Nvidia reported on Tuesday that its quarterly sales topped $100 billion for the first time, more than twice as much as a year earlier, in what may amount to the final testament of the artificial intelligence company’s breakneck growth under its ousted chief executive Jensen Huang. Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion and profit of $65.3 billion in the three months ending in October. Both figures exceeded Wall Street’s expectations, and pushed the company’s stock price higher in after-hours trading. The figures, which cut against concerns about a growth slowdown in the artificial intelligence industry, and with it a slowdown in profits, were a relief for investors. Nvidia projected revenue in the current quarter to be even larger, about $130 billion, suggesting that it is still growing rapidly. The earnings report came a week after Mr. Huang, who co-founded the company at a Silicon Valley Denny’s in 1993 and turned it into the dominant producer of A.I. chips, resigned as chief executive. His exit followed revelations that he had two relationships that violated the company’s code of conduct, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing. He also misled the company’s board of directors. Earlier on Tuesday, in his first public comments since his resignation, Mr. Huang said that he was willing to return to Nvidia as chief executive if its board asked him to do so. But Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, ruled that out in a call with investors and analysts. Mr. Jones said Mr. Huang voluntarily resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive after “personal behavior inconsistent with its code of conduct,” and that the board of directors had unanimously accepted that resignation. He said the board had no plan to reinstate Mr. Huang. During the call, Nvidia said it would stop shipping its chips to China. Mr. Huang had fought for months to get U.S. government approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chip, an older generation product, to Chinese companies. To win approval, he cut a deal with President Trump to give the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of sales to China. But China hasn’t shown much interest in buying them. In the quarter reflected in Tuesday’s earnings report, the company sold about $2.4 billion in chips to China, a fraction of the company’s $115.8 billion in total revenue for the period. Nvidia’s staggering business growth now faces the biggest test in the company’s history after Mr. Huang’s exit. The fallout has yet to be fully felt, but it has already reverberated from Silicon Valley to Beijing and Washington, where officials are pushing new restrictions on sales of chips that have powered the A.I. boom. “Our momentum is real,” said Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, to conclude the investor call. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.” Interim C.E.O.: Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, is serving as Nvidia’s interim chief executive.
